If the passage was fulfilled in the first century, it cannot prove that history ends in global apostasy, which removes a major objection to postmillennial optimism.

Amillennialists answer that the passage most naturally describes the time immediately before the final return, so its warning of apostasy contradicts the expectation of a Christianised world at the end.

The passage is strong evidence for a posttribulational rapture: Paul tells the church that the “gathering to him” (2:1) will not happen before the apostasy and the revelation of the man of lawlessness. The church will see the Antichrist, and Christ will destroy him at his coming. The restrainer is often identified as God's providential order (Roman law in Paul's day) rather than the church.

If believers were to be removed before the Antichrist appeared, Paul's simplest answer to the Thessalonians' fear would have been “you will be gone before then”. Instead he gives signs they will see first.

Pretribulationists argue that Paul's point is that the Day of the Lord (the tribulation) has not begun, which says nothing about the timing of the rapture itself. They also read the restrainer's removal as the church's removal.

The Thessalonians feared they were already in the Day of the Lord, the tribulation. Paul reassures them that it cannot begin until the restrainer, the Holy Spirit working through the church, is taken out of the way (ek mesou genētai) at the rapture. Some pretribulationists (E. Schuyler English, H. Wayne House, Thomas Ice) render apostasia as “departure”, meaning the rapture itself. The man of lawlessness is the future Antichrist, who will sit in a rebuilt Jerusalem temple.

Only a divine power could restrain Satan's working, and the neuter/masculine switch fits the Holy Spirit (pneuma is neuter in Greek, but the Spirit is a person). The comfort Paul gives (1 Thessalonians 5:9; 2 Thessalonians 2:13) suggests believers are not appointed to the wrath of that day.

Critics note that the text does not name the Spirit, that apostasia in the New Testament and the Greek Old Testament means rebellion or defection, not spatial departure (Acts 21:21), and that the Spirit could not be removed from the world while people are still being saved during the tribulation.

The man of sin is the papacy, a line of persons in an office, which sits in the church (the temple of God) claiming divine prerogatives. The restrainer was the pagan Roman empire, whose fall cleared the way for papal power. This reading is in the original Westminster Confession (25.6) and was common among the Reformers.

Historicists argue that the description of an apostasy within the church, centred in the “temple of God”, with a claim to sit in God's place, fits the papacy's development after Rome's fall better than any individual.

Critics say the passage describes an individual (“the man”, “the son of destruction”) destroyed at Christ's coming, not an institution lasting many centuries; many later Reformed bodies (for example the PCUSA in 1903) removed the identification from their confessions.

The coming of 2:1 and 2:8 is the parousia of AD 70. The man of lawlessness is a first-century figure (proposals include the Jewish high priestly establishment, Zealot leaders in the temple, or Nero), and the gathering of the saints and the destruction of the lawless one took place then.
Full preterists argue that the parousia of 2:1 and 2:8 should be the same coming as Matthew 24, which Jesus placed within his generation.

Critics answer that the “gathering” language links this passage to 1 Thessalonians 4:17, a bodily resurrection, which did not occur in AD 70. Partial preterists add that identifying the coming of 2:8 with AD 70 is possible without denying a future bodily return.
The Coming of the Lord and the Day of the Lord

Paul comforts grieving believers: at the coming (parousia) of the Lord, those who have died in Christ will rise first, then “we who are alive” will be caught up (harpagēsometha, Latin rapiemur, hence “rapture”) together with them in the clouds to meet (eis apantēsin) the Lord in the air. The Day of the Lord will come like a thief on the unprepared, but believers are children of the day and are not destined for wrath but for salvation.

Whether this “catching up” is a separate, pretribulational coming for the church or the single visible return (and whether apantēsis, a civic term for a delegation going out to escort a visiting dignitary back to the city, implies the saints return with Christ to earth). Also, whether “we who are alive” is a time statement, and whether 5:1-11 describes the same event as 4:13-18.

This is the rapture of the church, distinct from the Second Coming. Christ comes for his saints (in the air) before the seven-year tribulation, and later comes with them to earth (Zechariah 14:5; Revelation 19:14). The passage says nothing about tribulation signs, unlike Matthew 24, and the comfort Paul offers depends on the church being spared the Day of the Lord's wrath (5:9; 1:10). Prewrath advocates (Rosenthal) place the rapture later, inside the seventieth week but before God's wrath.

The language of comfort (4:18), the absence of any warning about the Antichrist, and the promise of deliverance from wrath (5:9) fit a rapture before the tribulation. Differences from Matthew 24 (resurrection, meeting in the air, no signs) suggest distinct events.

Critics answer that wrath in 5:9 means final condemnation, not the tribulation, and that Paul uses the same terms (parousia, trumpet, angel, clouds) as Jesus in Matthew 24:30-31 for a coming after the tribulation. Nothing in the text separates this coming from the visible return.

The rapture is the gathering of the church at Christ's single, visible, posttribulational return. Apantēsis describes a welcoming delegation that goes out to meet a visiting ruler and escorts him back, so believers rise to meet Christ and accompany him to earth to reign. The resurrection here is the first resurrection of Revelation 20:4-5, before the millennium.

The same word (apantēsis) is used in Matthew 25:6 and Acts 28:15 of people going out to meet someone and returning with them. The loud, public signals (a cry of command, an archangel's voice, God's trumpet) are hard to fit a secret event.

Pretribulationists argue that apantēsis need not have its technical sense here, and that the passage does not say where Christ and the church go after the meeting. They also argue that posttribulationism makes the rapture an odd up-and-down event.

This is the one future return of Christ, when all the dead in Christ are raised, living believers are transformed and caught up, and the final judgment and new creation follow. The Day of the Lord (5:2) is the same event from the side of the unbelieving world, which it overtakes with sudden destruction (5:3). There is no separate rapture and no intermediate millennium after it.

Paul treats the parousia and the Day of the Lord as one event with two sides: rescue for believers, destruction for unbelievers (compare 2 Thessalonians 1:6-10). Other texts tie the resurrection of believers to “the last day” (John 6:39-40).
Premillennialists reply that Paul mentions only the resurrection of believers here, which leaves room for the resurrection of the rest at a later point (Revelation 20:5).

Postmillennialists read the passage as amillennialists do: one visible return at the end of history, a general resurrection and the final judgment. Paul's “we who are alive” expresses solidarity with the whole church, not a prediction that the return would come within his lifetime. Most postmillennial partial preterists (Gentry, Mathison) regard this passage as still future.
Paul admits he does not know the time (5:1-2), and elsewhere he expects that he might die before the return (2 Corinthians 5:1-8; Philippians 1:21-23), so “we” is a general self-inclusion.
Full preterists argue that partial preterists are inconsistent: they accept the time texts of Matthew 24 as fulfilled in AD 70 but not Paul's “we who are alive”.

The parousia and gathering were fulfilled in AD 70. Paul expected the coming in his own generation (“we who are alive”), and it came as the spiritual and covenantal resurrection of God's people and their entrance into the presence of God, not a physical removal of bodies. The “Day of the Lord” was the destruction of Jerusalem.
Full preterists treat “we who are alive and remain” as a plain time statement, and link the trumpet and gathering to Matthew 24:31, which Jesus placed within his generation.

Critics argue that the text speaks of the dead rising and the living being caught up, which no one observed in AD 70, and that this reading denies the bodily resurrection confessed by all the historic creeds. Proponents answer that the resurrection is a covenantal, not biological, event.

All futurists place this event at the end of the age, but they divide on its timing relative to a future tribulation: pretribulational (before the seventieth week), midtribulational, prewrath (after the Antichrist's persecution but before God's wrath, after the sixth seal), and posttribulational (at the single return).
Each timing view reads 5:9 (not appointed to wrath) and the parallels with Matthew 24 and 2 Thessalonians 2 differently; the question is how much of the future tribulation counts as divine wrath.
Non-futurists argue the debate rests on a future seven-year tribulation that the text never mentions.
Each in His Own Order

Christ is the firstfruits (aparchē) of the resurrection; then (epeita) those who belong to Christ at his coming (parousia); then (eita) comes the end (to telos), when he hands over the kingdom to the Father after destroying every rule and power. He must reign until (achri hou) God has put all enemies under his feet (Psalm 110:1); the last enemy to be destroyed is death.

Whether there is a long interval between “then at his coming” and “then the end” (a millennium after the return), or whether the end comes at the parousia. Closely connected: when Christ's reign of 15:25 takes place. If it is now, at the Father's right hand, and ends at the return, there is no room for a later millennial reign; it also matters whether enemies are subdued before he returns.

Christ is reigning now from his ascension, and that reign must continue until all his enemies are subdued. Paul draws on Psalm 110:1: the session at the Father's right hand lasts until the enemies are a footstool. Every rule and authority is defeated during the present age, through the gospel, and only the last enemy, death, is destroyed at his return. Christ's parousia brings the end, not a further era.

Paul places the subduing of enemies within the reign that precedes the end, and he applies Psalm 110:1 to Christ's present session (as do Acts 2:34-35 and Hebrews 10:12-13). Death is abolished at the resurrection (15:54-55), so the return coincides with the end.

Amillennialists agree on the timing but argue that the subduing of enemies is decisively accomplished at the cross and finally at the return, not progressively in history. Premillennialists argue that “then the end” leaves room for a period after the return.

There are two stages in the resurrection: Christ, then his people at his coming. The end follows at that coming, with no millennium in between. Christ's reign (15:25) is his present heavenly reign, which lasts until the parousia, when death, the last enemy, is destroyed in the resurrection. A millennium after the return would mean that death continues after the resurrection, which Paul's sequence excludes.

In 15:54-55 the resurrection at the last trumpet is when “death is swallowed up in victory”. If death is destroyed at the return, there can be no subsequent age in which people still die (as premillennialists usually hold, compare Isaiah 65:20).
Premillennialists argue that eita (“then”) in 15:24 can indicate a gap, just as epeita in 15:23 covers the interval of nearly two thousand years between Christ's resurrection and the parousia.

Paul lists ordered stages: Christ the firstfruits, then believers at his coming, then the end. Since the first two are separated by a long period, the last two may be also, which makes room for the millennial reign of Revelation 20 between the parousia and the end. Ladd and others regard this as the clearest Pauline hint of a millennium.

The words epeita and eita both indicate succession, and the first interval is already about two thousand years. The final handing over of the kingdom to the Father (15:24) presupposes a period of the Son's rule.

Amillennialists and postmillennialists answer that the reign of 15:25 is located before the end by Psalm 110:1, which describes the present session, and that death being destroyed at the parousia excludes a later period in which death still operates.

Christ's reign in 15:25 includes his millennial reign on David's throne on earth after his return. The present session at the Father's right hand (Revelation 3:21 distinguishes “my throne” and “my Father's throne”) is not yet the Davidic reign, which begins at the Second Coming and ends when he hands the kingdom over after the millennium.
Distinguishing the Father's throne from Christ's own throne (Revelation 3:21; Matthew 25:31) suggests a future throne on earth. A gap between epeita and eita is possible on grammatical grounds.

Critics argue that Acts 2:30-36 places Christ on David's throne at his ascension (a point accepted by progressive dispensationalists such as Bock), and that the destruction of death at the parousia leaves no room for death during a later millennium.

Partial preterists, whether postmillennial or amillennial, regard this passage as describing a still-future bodily resurrection at Christ's final return, and treat it as the clearest refutation of full preterism. The parousia here is the coming that raises the dead and destroys death, which did not happen in AD 70.

The resurrection in 15:20-23 is modelled on Christ's own bodily resurrection (firstfruits of the same harvest), and death as the last enemy refers to physical death, as Paul's whole argument against those denying bodily resurrection (15:12) shows.

Full preterists answer that the context (15:56, “the power of sin is the law”) shows that the death in view is covenantal death under the law, which was abolished when the old covenant ended in AD 70.

The resurrection is corporate and covenantal: the “body” of God's people is raised from the death of the old Adamic and Mosaic covenant order into the life of the new covenant. That was completed at the parousia of AD 70, when Christ finished subduing his enemies and death, whose power was the law (15:56), was conquered. Max King's “covenant eschatology” develops this.
Proponents point to 15:56, which connects death's sting to sin and the law, and to the singular “body” (sōma) of 15:44, which they read corporately.

Critics argue that Paul's whole argument concerns individual bodily resurrection modelled on Christ's empty tomb (15:3-8, 12-20), that the creeds universally confess a future bodily resurrection, and that this view therefore lies outside historic Christian orthodoxy.
All Israel Will Be Saved

Paul reveals a mystery: a partial hardening (pōrōsis apo merous) has come upon Israel until (achri hou) the fullness (plērōma) of the Gentiles has come in, “and so” (kai houtōs) all Israel will be saved, as written in Isaiah 59:20-21 (the Deliverer will come from Zion). The broader passage (11:11-32) speaks of Israel's “fullness” bringing much greater blessing to the world (11:12) and of their acceptance meaning “life from the dead” (11:15). The gifts and calling of God are irrevocable (11:29).

What “all Israel” means: the whole church of Jews and Gentiles, the total of elect Jews across history, or the ethnic nation at a future point. Also: whether houtōs means “in this way” or (as many read it) implies a time sequence, and whether the coming of the Deliverer is the first or the second advent.

After the full number of Gentiles come in, there will be a widespread conversion of ethnic Jews to Christ, within history, before the end. That conversion will in turn bring great blessing to the world, “life from the dead” (11:15). This expectation fuelled the Puritan and evangelical missions movement (Edwards, the Puritans in Murray's study, Hodge).

Paul contrasts Israel's present partial hardening (“until”) with a future change, and promises that Israel's full inclusion will bring much greater blessing (11:12, 15), which suggests a historical sequence with further worldwide effects.

Critics say “life from the dead” may well refer to the final resurrection, which would place Israel's conversion at the end rather than before a further period of blessing. Others deny that the passage predicts a mass conversion at all.

Amillennialists are divided. Hoekema (and Merkle, Robertson, Berkhof) argues that “all Israel” means the total number of elect Jews throughout the age, gathered alongside Gentiles; “and so” refers to the manner of their salvation. Calvin read “all Israel” as the whole people of God. Others, such as Riddlebarger and Vos, expect a future large-scale conversion of Jews near the end, before the return.

Houtōs normally means “in this manner”, not “then”. Romans 9:6 distinguishes two senses of Israel, and 11:5 describes a present remnant, which suggests a continuing process rather than a single future event. The present tense of 11:31 (“that they now may receive mercy”) points to the present age.

Critics argue that in 11:25 “Israel” plainly means ethnic Israel, as distinct from Gentiles, and that a future conversion is the most natural reading of the contrast between present hardening and future salvation.

At or near Christ's return, the Deliverer coming from Zion, there will be a large-scale turning of ethnic Israel to Christ. Historic premillennialists hold that Israel and the church become one people in Christ, but that God has a future for the Jewish people, who will enter the millennial kingdom.
Paul quotes Isaiah 59:20, which can be read of the Second Coming, and Moo and others regard a large end-time conversion of ethnic Israel as the most natural reading.
Others reply that Paul's quotation may describe Christ's first coming and the removal of sin through the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:33-34), not a future event.

The passage is a key text for God's distinct future for national Israel. After the church age, the time of the Gentiles' fullness, national Israel will repent and turn to its Messiah at the Second Coming (compare Zechariah 12:10). This will lead to the fulfilment of the land and kingdom promises in the millennium, since the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable (11:29).

Paul distinguishes Israel and the Gentiles throughout Romans 11, and irrevocable promises (11:28-29) seem to include the national and territorial covenants. The olive tree image (11:17-24) assumes natural branches can be grafted back.
Critics argue that Paul speaks of salvation, forgiveness and inclusion in the olive tree with Gentiles, not territorial promises or a separate future programme for Israel.

Partial preterists vary. Many, following postmillennial tradition, expect a future conversion of the Jews. Some see the context in the first-century mission and the AD 70 crisis, with N. T. Wright (often grouped with preterist readings of the Gospels) arguing that “all Israel” is the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile, completed through the gospel.

Wright points to Paul's redefinition of Israel around Christ (Romans 2:28-29; 9:6; Galatians 6:16), and to the quotation of Isaiah 59 with “from Zion” rather than “for Zion”, suggesting the Deliverer goes out from Zion to the nations.
Critics argue that the shift from “Israel” meaning ethnic Jews in 11:25 to “all Israel” meaning the church in 11:26 is abrupt and unlikely within the same sentence.

Progressive covenantalists (Wellum, Gentry) hold that Christ is the true Israel and that the land promises are fulfilled typologically in the new creation. Many still allow, with Moo and Schreiner, that Romans 11 predicts a future large-scale salvation of ethnic Jews, who are joined to the one people of God rather than given a separate national programme.
This reading accepts a future for ethnic Jews while treating the covenants as fulfilled in Christ, which they argue fits both Romans 11 and Ephesians 2:11-22.

Dispensationalists argue that it promises Israel salvation but not the specific national restoration of the prophets. Covenant theologians argue that it adds little to the Reformed amillennial or postmillennial view.

The salvation of all Israel was completed at the parousia of AD 70, when the Deliverer came out of (heavenly) Zion and the covenant promises were fulfilled. “All Israel” is the faithful remnant together with believing Gentiles.
Full preterists connect the quotation of Isaiah 59:20 to the coming in judgment and salvation that Jesus placed within his generation.
Critics say there is no evidence of a large-scale salvation of Jews in AD 70; on the contrary, the destruction of Jerusalem was a judgment on unbelief.
The Lord's Anointed

The nations rage and their rulers plot against the LORD and his anointed. God laughs, having installed his king on Zion. The king announces God's decree, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you”, and the promise of the nations as his inheritance, to be broken with a rod of iron. The kings are warned to serve the LORD and “kiss the Son”.

When the Son receives the nations and rules them with the rod. The New Testament applies 2:1-2 to the crucifixion (Acts 4:25-27) and 2:7 to the resurrection (Acts 13:33; Hebrews 1:5), but Revelation applies the rod of iron to Christ's return and to the reign of the saints (Revelation 2:26-27; 12:5; 19:15).

The Son was installed as king at his resurrection and ascension and is now claiming the nations given to him as an inheritance (2:8) through the preaching of the gospel. The psalm summons rulers to submit to Christ in history (2:10-12), which postmillennialists see as a mandate and a promise that nations, not just individuals, will be discipled.
Acts 13:33 places the decree of 2:7 at the resurrection, so the inheritance is offered now. The call to kings to serve the LORD is addressed to rulers within history, before judgment.
Critics answer that the rod of iron in Revelation 19:15 is applied to Christ's return, which shows that the decisive subjugation of the nations is at the end, not progressively in history.

Christ was enthroned on the heavenly Zion at his resurrection and ascension (Hebrews 12:22) and reigns now. The nations' rebellion continues throughout this age, and the rod of iron describes his final judgment at the return, as well as the present triumph of his people (Revelation 2:26-27).

The New Testament applies the psalm to the crucifixion, resurrection and exaltation, which places the king's installation in the past and the judgment in the future, without an intervening millennium.
Postmillennialists argue that this underplays the promise of the nations as an inheritance; premillennialists argue that it removes the earthly dimension of the rule from Zion.

Christ was declared Son at the resurrection, but his rule over the nations with a rod of iron awaits his return and the millennial kingdom, in which the saints share it (Revelation 2:26-27). The psalm thus spans the first and second advents.
Revelation 2:26-27 promises the overcomers authority over the nations with an iron rod, which premillennialists read as their reign in the millennium after the return (Revelation 20:4).
Amillennialists argue that Revelation 2:27 describes the saints sharing Christ's victory, already begun, not a future earthly reign.

Classical dispensationalists hold that Christ is not yet reigning on David's throne on Zion; the installation and rod of iron are fulfilled at the Second Coming, when he rules the nations from Jerusalem in the millennium. Progressive dispensationalists (Bock, Blaising) argue that the Davidic reign was inaugurated at the resurrection (Acts 2; 13), with the earthly rule from Zion still future.
The psalm speaks of an earthly Zion and of crushing the rebellious nations, which dispensationalists argue has not happened yet.
Critics say the New Testament's own use of the psalm (Acts 4:25-27; 13:33) places the installation at the resurrection, and Hebrews 12:22 identifies the Zion of the new covenant as heavenly.

The rulers raging against the anointed include Herod, Pilate and the leaders of Israel (Acts 4:25-27). The warning of 2:12 (that his wrath is quickly kindled) was carried out against unbelieving Jerusalem in AD 70, and the Son continues to receive the nations in the gospel age.
Acts 4 explicitly applies 2:1-2 to the first-century authorities, and Jesus warned those same authorities of imminent judgment (Matthew 23:36).
Critics say the psalm's horizon is universal (all the nations, the ends of the earth), so AD 70 is at most a partial instance, not the fulfilment.
Sit at My Right Hand

The LORD says to David's Lord, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool.” The LORD will extend his mighty sceptre from Zion; he rules in the midst of his enemies; his people offer themselves willingly in the day of his power; he is a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek, and will shatter kings and judge among the nations. It is the Old Testament text most often quoted or alluded to in the New Testament.

What happens during the session at the right hand. The New Testament places Christ's enthronement at his ascension (Acts 2:34-36; Hebrews 1:13; 10:12-13). The question is whether the subduing of enemies “until” the footstool is complete happens progressively during this age, all at once at the return, or after the return in a millennium.

Christ is now seated at the right hand and will remain there until his enemies are made his footstool. He rules “in the midst of his enemies” (110:2), and his people volunteer freely in the day of his power (110:3). The subjugation of enemies therefore happens in history, through the gospel, before he returns, and his return comes after that victory.

Hebrews 10:12-13 pictures Christ seated, waiting until his enemies are made a footstool, which places their subjugation during the session. Paul uses the same psalm to describe the reign that ends in the end (1 Corinthians 15:25).

Amillennialists answer that the enemies are made a footstool in a final, decisive act at the return (compare 2 Thessalonians 1:7-9), not by gradual conversion of the world. Rule “in the midst of enemies” suggests ongoing opposition.

Christ's session at the right hand is his present messianic reign, the millennium of Revelation 20. He rules now from the heavenly Zion through his word and Spirit, in the midst of enemies who will finally be subdued at his return and the last judgment. The psalm leaves no room for another reign after his return; at that point he hands the kingdom to the Father (1 Corinthians 15:24-28).
Acts 2:34-36 announces Christ's enthronement as fulfilling the psalm, and Peter connects it with David's throne (Acts 2:30), which makes the present session the promised messianic reign.

Postmillennialists argue that this does not take seriously the progressive conquest implied in the psalm. Premillennialists argue that the session at the right hand is distinct from Christ's own kingdom on earth.

Christ reigns now at the right hand, which is a real inauguration of his kingdom. The subjugation of his enemies will be completed in stages: at his return he will judge the nations and reign on earth (110:5-6), and at the end of the millennium the last enemy, death, will be destroyed.

The psalm moves from session (110:1) to judgment of kings and nations (110:5-6), which premillennialists see as a sequence beginning with the session and ending with a visible conquest, matching Revelation 19-20.
Critics argue that 1 Corinthians 15:25-26 places the destruction of death at the end of the session, so there is no period after the session in which death continues.

Classical dispensationalists (Walvoord) distinguish the Father's throne, where Christ sits now as priest, from the Davidic throne he will occupy on earth after his return; the rule from Zion (110:2) is millennial. Progressive dispensationalists (Bock) accept that the Davidic reign was inaugurated at the ascension, according to Acts 2:30-36, but hold that its fulfilment on earth, in relation to Israel and the nations, is still future.
Revelation 3:21 distinguishes Christ's throne from his Father's throne. The psalm's concrete judgment of kings and nations awaits his visible return.
Critics argue that Acts 2 applies the psalm to Christ's present reign as David's heir, which makes a separate future Davidic throne unnecessary.

The session ended in AD 70, when his enemies (unbelieving Jerusalem and the old covenant order) were made his footstool and the day of his wrath (110:5) came. Christ reigns over a kingdom now fully established.
Full preterists connect Jesus' warning to the high priest (Mark 14:62, citing Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13) with the judgment within that generation.
Critics argue that death, the last enemy, has not been abolished, and that Paul places the subjugation of all enemies (including death) at the general resurrection.
The Mountain of the LORD's House

“In the latter days” (beʾacharit hayyamim) the mountain of the LORD's house will be established as the highest of the mountains. All nations will stream to it to learn God's ways; instruction (torah) will go out from Zion; he will judge between the nations, and they will beat their swords into plowshares and learn war no more. Micah 4:1-3 has the same oracle.

When the latter days are and what the mountain is. The New Testament says the last days began with Christ (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2). The question is whether the oracle is fulfilled progressively in the church now, in a literal millennial Jerusalem after the return, or in the final new creation.

The latter days began with Christ's first coming. The mountain is the exalted kingdom of God, the heavenly Zion to which the church has come (Hebrews 12:22), and the nations are now streaming to it through the gospel. As this continues, the word of God will increasingly shape nations and international relations, bringing a real, if not perfect, era of peace before Christ returns.
